Passage A

[1] On Sunday nights my father and I carried the week down three flights of stairs in two pillowcases, and the walk to the Spin Cycle on Delancey took eleven minutes if the light at the corner was kind. I was nine, then ten, then eleven, and for those three years the laundromat was the only place I ever saw him sit still.

[2] He was a man who fixed things—radiators, other people's cars, the tempers of my older cousins—and at home there was always a next thing waiting with its hands on its hips. But at the Spin Cycle the machines did the work, and there was nothing for him to do but feed quarters into the slot and wait. He would take the orange plastic chair nearest the window, tip it back against the glass, and read the free weekly paper from the front page to the classifieds, including the ads for apartments we could not afford.

[3] I did my homework on the folding table, which smelled of bleach and someone else's dryer sheets. When the wash finished, he taught me to sort: the towels to the big dryer, the shirts to the medium one, and my school blouses to a third machine set on low, because the small dryer had once shrunk one and he had never forgiven it. He counted the quarters out in stacks of four. I understood, without being told, that the stacks were a kind of arithmetic about the week.

[4] There were other regulars—a nurse who came in scrubs, an old man who folded his undershirts into perfect squares and never spoke—but we did not talk to them, and they did not talk to us. That was the arrangement. It was a room full of people agreeing to be alone together for ninety minutes, and I found it unaccountably restful.

[5] I have my own machine now, in a closet off the kitchen, and it runs while I do other things, and I never sit and watch it. I have tried to explain to my daughter why the Spin Cycle stays with me, and the closest I can get is this: it was the one hour of the week when nothing was being asked of my father, and so nothing was being asked of me either. We were simply two people waiting for the towels to be dry. I did not know then that this was rare. I thought every family had a place like that.

Passage B

[1] I took over the Wash-n-Fold on Ninth Street from my uncle in 1994, and for twenty-six years I opened it at six and closed it at ten, and in that time I learned that people will tell a laundromat attendant things they would not tell their priest. It is the waiting that does it. Nobody plans to talk; the machines simply give them forty minutes with nothing in their hands.

[2] I kept the place clean, because a dirty laundromat is a contradiction, and I kept the change machine full, because an empty one is a betrayal. Beyond that I tried to be furniture. I read at the counter. I did not look up when the door opened unless someone needed me. The regulars, I found, wanted exactly that: to be known and left alone in the same gesture.

[3] There was a man who came in with a young girl every Sunday for a few years—she did her schoolwork on my folding table, he read my newspaper front to back—and in all that time we exchanged perhaps a hundred words, most of them about the small dryer, which ran hot. When they stopped coming I assumed they had moved, or bought a machine, which is how it usually ends. I thought about them more than a hundred words should justify.

[4] People assume a laundromat is a sad place, and I will not pretend that no one ever cried at my folding table. But I saw a great deal more of the other thing. I saw a woman teach her son to fold a fitted sheet, which is a skill I myself never mastered. I saw two strangers argue about a ballgame on my television for an hour and shake hands at the door. I saw, on a Tuesday afternoon in February, an old man who never spoke to anyone leave a stack of quarters on top of the machine a young mother had been counting out coins for, and walk out before she noticed.

[5] The building sold in 2020 and the new owner wanted a juice bar, and I did not fight it, because I was tired and the lease said what it said. I still walk past. It is very bright in there now, and everyone is looking at a phone, and no one is waiting for anything. I do not think that is worse, exactly. But I think something is lost when a neighborhood has no room in it where people are obliged to sit still with strangers, and I was proud, for twenty-six years, to keep one.

prompt: As it is used in the sentence "It was a room full of people agreeing to be alone together for ninety minutes, and I found it unaccountably restful", the word unaccountably most nearly means:
choices: irresponsibly.
unreliably.
inexplicably.
unaffordably.
correct_answer: inexplicably.
explanation: The narrator is reporting a feeling she cannot fully explain: that a room of silent strangers should feel restful is surprising, so the restfulness is inexplicable. The other senses of "unaccountable" (not answerable, not dependable) and the unrelated "unaffordably" do not fit a description of a feeling.

[1] When the last grocery store in a small town closes, the event is usually reported as a loss of convenience: residents must now drive twenty or thirty miles for fresh milk. But economists who study rural retail describe the closure as something closer to a structural event, one that changes what kind of place the town can be. A grocery store is the anchor tenant of a main street. It generates daily trips, and daily trips are what keep the pharmacy, the hardware store, and the diner alive. When the anchor goes, the others tend to follow within a decade.

[2] The arithmetic behind these closures is unforgiving. A full-service grocery store operates on a net margin of roughly one to three percent, which means it survives on volume. A store serving a town of 1,500 people, most of whom already drive to a regional center once a week for work or errands, cannot generate the volume that its wholesaler's minimum orders and its refrigeration bills assume. Between 1990 and 2015, by one widely cited estimate, the number of independent grocers in towns under 2,500 people fell by nearly half. The stores that survived were disproportionately those that owned their buildings outright and whose proprietors were willing to accept what amounted to a below-minimum wage for their own labor.

[3] Into this vacuum came the small-format discount chain. These stores—typically 8,000 to 10,000 square feet, staffed by three or four employees, and stocked mainly with packaged and shelf-stable goods—can operate profitably in towns a supermarket cannot. Their expansion into rural counties over the past two decades has been remarkable: in some Plains states, there is now a discount store within fifteen miles of nearly every resident. For a household that needs paper towels and canned soup, this is a genuine improvement. For a household that needs a head of lettuce, it is not, because most of these stores carry no fresh produce and little fresh meat.

[4] Whether the discounters cause grocery closures or merely arrive after them is a contested question. Studies that compare towns before and after a discounter opens find that existing grocers lose between five and fifteen percent of their sales in the first two years, which for a store already at the margin can be decisive. Critics of this research point out that discounters choose their locations carefully and may simply be good at identifying towns whose grocers were already failing. The most careful recent work suggests both things are true at once: the chains target vulnerable markets, and their arrival accelerates the outcome they anticipated.

[5] What has attracted the attention of policymakers is not the closures themselves but the range of responses that towns have improvised. Some have offered tax abatements to lure a regional chain, usually without success, since the abatement does not change the underlying volume problem. Others have turned to models that were, until recently, considered exotic. A handful of towns now operate municipally owned grocery stores, financed by sales-tax revenue and run by a city employee. A larger number have organized cooperatives, in which residents buy shares and elect a board. And a few school districts have opened stores staffed partly by students, treating the enterprise as both a service and a vocational program.

[6] The results are mixed and the sample is small, but a pattern has begun to emerge. Municipal and cooperative stores rarely turn a profit in the conventional sense; most require an ongoing subsidy or volunteer labor to stay open. Judged as businesses, they fail. Judged as infrastructure—the way a town judges its water system or its road grader—they look different. One survey of twelve community-owned stores found that residents who used them made an average of 1.8 fewer out-of-town trips per week, and that the towns' remaining businesses reported modest but consistent increases in foot traffic after the store opened. The subsidy, in other words, was buying something, even if the store's own ledger did not show it.

[7] This reframing—from business to infrastructure—is where the debate now sits. Skeptics argue that a town of 1,200 people cannot indefinitely tax itself to keep a store open, and that the honest response to depopulation is to accept it rather than fight it one storefront at a time. Advocates reply that the same logic would have removed rural electrification and rural mail delivery, both of which were also unprofitable and both of which are now regarded as obviously worth their cost. Neither side disputes the underlying figures. What they disagree about is which ledger a town should be reading.

[1] For roughly a century, from the 1870s to the 1950s, the American house had a face, and the face had a mouth. The front porch—a roofed platform raised a few steps above the yard, deep enough for chairs, open to the street—was so nearly universal in that period that its absence on a new house required explanation. Pattern books sold to builders assumed it. Mail-order house kits shipped its columns in numbered crates. In the towns of the Midwest and South especially, a street was less a row of houses than a row of porches, each one occupied, on a summer evening, by people who could see and be seen.

[2] The porch did not begin as a social instrument. Its ancestors were practical: the verandas of colonial outposts in hot climates, where a roofed perimeter kept sun off the walls and let air move through open doors; the stoops of Dutch townhouses, where a raised entry kept floodwater out. What the nineteenth century did was to take these functional appendages and enlarge them until they became rooms without walls, and then to furnish them—with swings, rockers, and wicker—until they became rooms one was expected to sit in.

[3] Sitting in them had rules, though no one wrote the rules down. A person on a porch was at home and yet available. A neighbor walking past could call a greeting and expect one back; could stop at the foot of the steps and talk for a while; could, if invited, come up and take a chair. Each of these stages carried a different degree of intimacy, and the architecture made the gradations legible. The steps were a threshold; the railing was a boundary that permitted conversation across it; the front door, behind the porch, was a second and more serious threshold that most passersby would never cross. The porch was where the private household and the public street negotiated their terms.

[4] The historian Ruth Ambler, whose work on domestic architecture has shaped most recent discussion of the subject, puts the point in a way that has been quoted so often it has become almost a proverb: "The porch was never a room. It was a sentence the house spoke to the street, and when we stopped building porches we did not fall silent so much as change the subject." Her argument is that the porch's decline should be read not as a loss of sociability but as a redirection of it—toward the backyard, the automobile, and eventually the screen.

[5] The decline itself was swift. Three changes, arriving together in the decades after the Second World War, made the porch first unnecessary and then undesirable. Air conditioning removed the reason to sit outside on a hot evening. The automobile transformed the street from a place people walked through into a place they drove through, and a porch facing a stream of cars offered neither quiet nor company. And television gave the household a new focal point, one located in the interior and demanding darkness. Builders of postwar subdivisions, working to tight budgets and fast schedules, dropped the porch almost overnight and replaced it with a token stoop or nothing at all. The back patio, walled by fence and shrubbery, took over its furniture and abandoned its audience.

[6] Ambler's reading has not gone unchallenged. Some scholars object that "changing the subject" understates what was lost: a backyard patio may host the same barbecue, but it does not permit the unplanned, low-stakes contact with neighbors that the porch made routine, and it is precisely that kind of contact, they argue, that builds the trust a neighborhood runs on. Others note that the porch's golden age was also an age of intense social surveillance, in which being visible from the street meant being judged from it, and that the privacy of the patio was for many households a relief rather than a loss.

[7] The porch's partial return since the 1990s complicates the story further. Planned communities built on so-called traditional principles now require porches of a specified depth, and the porches are duly built. But visitors to these developments often report that the porches sit empty. Critics of the revival suggest that this is because a porch is not a cause of neighborliness but a symptom of it: the nineteenth-century porch was occupied because the street was already full of people worth greeting, and building the platform does not summon the parade. Defenders reply that habits take longer than a decade to form, and that the children now growing up in front of these porches may use them as their grandparents did.

[8] What both sides accept is Ambler's underlying insight, that a house is an argument about how its occupants wish to meet the world. The porch made one argument. The garage door, which now occupies the position on the facade that the porch once held, makes another. Whether the newer argument is worse is a question about which reasonable people differ; that it is different, no one seriously disputes.

The front porch—a roofed platform raised a few steps above the yard, deep enough for chairs, open to the street—was so nearly universal in that period that its absence on a new house required explanation. Pattern books sold to builders assumed it. Mail-order house kits shipped its columns in numbered crates. In the towns of the Midwest and South especially, a street was less a row of houses than a row of porches, each one occupied, on a summer evening, by people who could see and be seen.

[2] The porch did not begin as a social instrument. Its ancestors were practical: the verandas of colonial outposts in hot climates, where a roofed perimeter kept sun off the walls and let air move through open doors; the stoops of Dutch townhouses, where a raised entry kept floodwater out. What the nineteenth century did was to take these functional appendages and enlarge them until they became rooms without walls, and then to furnish them—with swings, rockers, and wicker—until they became rooms one was expected to sit in.

[3] Sitting in them had rules, though no one wrote the rules down. A person on a porch was at home and yet available. A neighbor walking past could call a greeting and expect one back; could stop at the foot of the steps and talk for a while; could, if invited, come up and take a chair. Each of these stages carried a different degree of intimacy, and the architecture made the gradations legible. The steps were a threshold; the railing was a boundary that permitted conversation across it; the front door, behind the porch, was a second and more serious threshold that most passersby would never cross. The porch was where the private household and the public street negotiated their terms.

[4] The historian Ruth Ambler, whose work on domestic architecture has shaped most recent discussion of the subject, puts the point in a way that has been quoted so often it has become almost a proverb: "The porch was never a room. It was a sentence the house spoke to the street, and when we stopped building porches we did not fall silent so much as change the subject." Her argument is that the porch's decline should be read not as a loss of sociability but as a redirection of it—toward the backyard, the automobile, and eventually the screen.

[5] The decline itself was swift. Three changes, arriving together in the decades after the Second World War, made the porch first unnecessary and then undesirable. Air conditioning removed the reason to sit outside on a hot evening. The automobile transformed the street from a place people walked through into a place they drove through, and a porch facing a stream of cars offered neither quiet nor company. And television gave the household a new focal point, one located in the interior and demanding darkness. Builders of postwar subdivisions, working to tight budgets and fast schedules, dropped the porch almost overnight and replaced it with a token stoop or nothing at all. The back patio, walled by fence and shrubbery, took over its furniture and abandoned its audience.

[1] A hummingbird weighs about as much as a nickel, and that fact governs almost everything about how it lives. Small animals have a great deal of surface area relative to their volume, and surface is where heat escapes. A hummingbird at rest on a mild day must burn energy at a rate that, scaled to human size, would require a person to eat roughly their own body weight in food each day. During the daylight hours the bird meets this demand by feeding almost continuously, visiting hundreds of flowers and consuming more than its own mass in nectar. At night, when it cannot feed, the arithmetic turns against it.

[2] The problem is sharpest at high elevation. In the Andes, several hummingbird species live and breed above 3,500 meters, where nighttime temperatures routinely fall below freezing even in the breeding season. A bird that maintained its daytime body temperature of about 40 degrees Celsius through a ten-hour night at minus five would exhaust its fat reserves before dawn. Some individuals would not survive a single night. Yet these species are not rare; some are among the most common birds of the high grasslands.

[3] The solution is torpor, a controlled and reversible drop in body temperature and metabolic rate. A torpid hummingbird is not asleep in the ordinary sense. Its heart rate, which may exceed 1,000 beats per minute in flight, falls to a few dozen. Its breathing becomes irregular and may pause for a minute at a time. Its body temperature drops toward that of the surrounding air, and the energy it spends maintaining itself falls with it. A bird that would burn a given amount of fat holding 40 degrees may burn a small fraction of that amount holding 10. The difference is what gets it to morning.

[4] For decades, researchers assumed that torpor in hummingbirds was shallow and that the birds stopped cooling at a floor somewhere in the high teens or low twenties Celsius, below which some vital process would fail. Field studies of high-Andean species conducted over the past decade have overturned that assumption. Using tiny temperature probes and small cages placed at the birds' own roost sites, one team recorded overnight body temperatures in six species, identified here by letter. Their measurements are summarized in the table below.

Species | Body mass (g) | Lowest recorded body temperature (°C) | Estimated overnight energy saving (%)
A | 6.0 | 3.3 | 95
B | 8.2 | 6.1 | 91
C | 4.4 | 9.8 | 86
D | 8.0 | 16.5 | 70
E | 20.5 | 21.0 | 61
F | 7.5 | 12.2 | 79

[5] Species A's 3.3 degrees was the lowest body temperature the team had ever seen reported for a bird, and it was recorded in a bird that flew off the next morning. The measurement forced a revision not only of what hummingbirds can do but of what a functioning bird body is. At 3.3 degrees, most enzyme reactions have slowed to a crawl; the heart is beating perhaps thirty times a minute; the animal is, by any casual inspection, dead. That it is not dead—that it can rewarm itself by shivering, at a rate of about one degree per minute, and be feeding within half an hour of sunrise—suggests that the machinery of the bird is built with margins that its daytime life never reveals.

[6] The table also shows something the researchers had not expected. Energy saving does not track body mass in a simple way. Species E, at more than twenty grams, cooled least and saved least, which fits the general rule that larger bodies lose heat more slowly and therefore have less to gain from torpor. But among the small species, depth of torpor varied by more than ten degrees between birds of similar size, and the differences appeared to be tied to where each species roosted rather than to how much it weighed. The species that cooled furthest were those that roost in the open, on exposed branches or cliff faces. Those that sheltered in cavities or dense vegetation—where the air around them stayed several degrees warmer—did not cool as far, and did not need to.

[7] This last finding has shifted how biologists think about torpor. It had been treated as a property of species, a fixed physiological setting that a given kind of bird either had or lacked. The Andean data suggest that it is better understood as a strategy—that a bird chooses, each night, how deep to go, and that the choice depends on its fat reserves, the temperature of its roost, and perhaps on how much it expects to find to eat the next day. Captive birds fed to satiation in the evening enter torpor later and less deeply than birds allowed to go to roost hungry. The bird, in other words, is doing a version of the arithmetic described at the start of this passage, and adjusting its night accordingly.

[8] Torpor is not free. A torpid bird cannot flee a predator, and a bird that misjudges and cools too far may lack the reserves to rewarm. The prevalence of deep torpor in high-Andean species is therefore itself evidence: it shows that the nightly risk of freezing outweighed, over evolutionary time, the nightly risk of being eaten. The nickel-weight bird on the frozen branch is not a marvel of endurance so much as a very small accountant, balancing two dangers in the dark.
